A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same channel-wise influence method and its anomaly-detection and channel-pruning applications. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite renaming and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original anomaly-detection, forecasting and channel-pruning experiments, including architecture generalization and selection-strategy analyses in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, an ETTh1 case study, sample-pruning comparisons and additional forecasting and runtime results.

M1.justification: The gradient-based influence score, maximum channel self-influence anomaly score and equidistant pruning strategy remain. Algorithm 2 corrects its selection condition from i == t to i mod t == 0, making the pseudocode implement the periodic selection already described in v1. This is a limited algorithm correction; the PDFs do not establish a changed experimental implementation.

E1.justification: All original anomaly-detection and forecasting datasets remain. v2 adds ETTh1 and ETTm1, extending pruning evaluation to seven-channel transformer datasets, including an ETTh1 interpretability case study. The underlying anomaly-detection and forecasting tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds TimeInf to the anomaly-detection comparison and LIME, SHAP and NFS to the main channel-pruning comparison. Random channel selection is removed from that corresponding 96-step comparison, although retained in other experiments. Figure 3 additionally compares channel pruning against MoSo and random sample pruning, substantially expanding the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.2.3 introduces a substantive evaluation design comparing sample and channel pruning at matched retained-data proportions. Additional protocols include 192-step forecasting, DLinear as a forecasting backbone, retaining two or three ETT channels, and per-instance or per-timestamp timing measurements. Existing main experiments retain their stated metrics, optimizers and input windows.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ETTh1 case study examining whether selected channels represent distinct physical variables, sample-versus-channel pruning analysis, and runtime/scaling analyses. Appendix D.4 also extends generalization checks to DLinear and longer forecasts. The original gradient-parameter ablation, architecture-generalization results and equidistant-versus-most-influential selection study are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experiments. Mean/standard-deviation and median/IQR calculations concern the unchanged anomaly-score normalization procedure, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Most matched original scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial baseline, pruning, ETT, 192-step, DLinear and runtime results. New comparisons reveal exceptions to ChInf's lead: in Table 3, iTransformer on Solar at 20% retention scores 0.214 with LIME versus 0.219 with ChInf. PatchTST full-channel reference MSE also changes from 0.224 to 0.223 on Solar and 0.454 to 0.452 on Traffic between v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 3, without an explanation.

T1.justification: v2 reverses the loss difference defining TracIn in Equation 1 and the appendix proof, and explicitly describes the reference model as trained without the studied example. Appendix D.6 adds an O(nd) computational-complexity argument. The channel-wise decomposition remains; the proof's intermediate Taylor-expansion sign is still inconsistent with the revised loss difference.

C1.justification: The first channel-wise influence claim and the anomaly-detection/channel-pruning contributions remain. v2 adds the explicit conclusion that channel pruning removes more redundant data than sample-wise pruning, and foregrounds dataset redundancy and insufficient data utilization by current models. These extend the conclusions within the existing research scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's general limitation about unexplored tasks, v2 specifically discusses strengths on localized channel faults and possible weakness on globally synchronized anomalies. It adds a temporal-dependence explanation for MoSo's performance, physical interpretations of selected ETTh1 channels, and explanations of differences from LIME and SHAP. These substantially expand mechanism discussions and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies a code-repository link and clarifies that anomaly-detection metrics on SMD, MSL and SMAP are computed per trace and then averaged. It also documents the units of work used for timing measurements. The existing PyTorch, RTX 3090, optimizer, loss and window-length disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning by acknowledging TimeInf and distinguishing temporal influence from channel-wise influence. It expands connections to dataset pruning, including language-model data pruning, and contrasts ChInf with LIME, SHAP and NFS. Additional anomaly-detection references support the new applicability discussion; these changes go beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and the method is consistently presented as ChInf. Section 4.2 is reorganized around dataset pruning, the pruning experiments gain a subsection structure, and broader impact and dataset descriptions move into the appendices. The title, author block and section terminology also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a conference layout and places the algorithms side by side. It removes the original framework diagram, moves and enlarges the anomaly-score visualization, relocates dataset tables and condenses the main architecture-generalization table while retaining full appendix results. New displays include ETTh1 traces, sample-pruning curves, a summary of existing retention ratios, and additional forecasting and runtime tables.

improvement.justification: v1's main pruning validation relied on naive channel selectors. v2 addresses this important evidence gap through LIME/SHAP/NFS comparisons and direct sample-pruning comparisons, while TimeInf supplies a relevant time-series influence baseline. Runtime measurements and specific anomaly-type limitations further improve practical assessment. Some new table highlighting overstates ChInf's wins, the proof retains a sign inconsistency, and uncertainty remains unreported, but the comparative evidence is substantially stronger overall.
